Cemair

By: Graham Coetzer | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Last week low cost airline Cemair was grounded by the Civil Aviation Authority over concerns about aircraft safety but that's only the beginning - we expose their lethal history

Unique Selling Point:
Last year three ex-Cemair pilots approached Carte Blanche about the malpractice in the company. They allege Cemair forces pilots to fly in dangerous conditions, and if they speak up about it they get the axe. Allegations range from aircraft being overweight prior to takeoff, a huge no-no in the aviation industry, to aircraft landing on runways they are not certified to land on, to lack of proper maintenance on the aircraft. They have supplied us with emails and documentation corroborating their stories.

Summary:
Cemair CEO Miles van der Molen has a particularly bad history in SA aviation. Three aircraft that we know of, and were flying under various companies van der Molen owns, have crashed and resulted in fatalities. One of those cases was an aircraft that fell at OR Tambo International killing the two occupants. Another case resulted in an aircraft crashing seconds after takeoff at Rand Airport, where the two pilots, one cabin crew and 13 passengers all died. The civil aviation authority found the aircraft to be overweight and not properly maintained. The latest drama has seen Cemair grounded for allegedly falsifying aircraft maintenance reports, having them signed off by unqualified individuals. It is clear that van der Molen likes cutting corners to protect the businesses bottom line, but in aviation that means putting lives at stake.

Press Release:


CemAir Grounded
Last week local airline CemAir had several of its aircraft grounded due to questions around their airworthiness certificates. With flights suspended, frustrated passengers scurried to make alternative arrangements. In a statement CemAir said they were hopeful that they’d be taking to the skies soon, but insiders say that’s only the beginning of their problems. Carte Blanche investigates.


Script:


CemAir
08 February 2018

Voice
Last week Friday, the South African Civil Aviation Authority grounded 12 of local airline CemAir’s aircraft. The CAA withdrew their Certificates of Airworthiness after their annual audit found that unqualified personnel at CemAir had cleared the aircraft as airworthy. Simon Segwabe is the executive: Aviation Safety Operations at the CAA.

Sound Up Simon Segwabe CAA
That was followed by us communicating with the operator, to say our inspection has revealed these deficiencies, which are on your craft. We therefore won’t be able to allow your aircraft to operate further, until these deficiencies have been addressed.

Voice
Because the CAA’s annual Maintenance Review Report raised questions around the maintenance of CemAir’s aircraft, the regulator is now comparing the maintenance documents to the actual work done on the aircraft.

Sound Up Simon
We then take those documentation and verify with the actual aircraft if that maintenance was conducted.

Voice
CemAir is wholly owned by CEO Miles van der Molen. They operate a domestic passenger service out of OR Tambo and fly to destinations like Margate, Bloemfontein and Plettenburg Bay. They also operate in several African countries, like Sudan and Mali. Van der Molen says his maintenance staff are qualified for the job.

Sound Up Miles van der Molen
Miles: He is a qualified, licensed engineer. The question isn’t whether he’s qualified or not, the question is whether he is eligible in terms of the documentation to sign off on a certificate of release.

Devi: Is he eligible?

Miles: We believe he is in terms of our documentation.

Devi: And they’re saying?

Miles: They’re saying he is not.

Voice
van der Molen says it’s simply a matter of semantics.

Sound Up Miles
We don’t believe it’s a safety issue, we believe its a compliance issue.

Voice
But that’s not what the CAA say.

Sound UP Simon Segwabe
It is a safety issue, safety in this manner. An aircraft is represented by certain documents post maintenance, because that demonstrates to us what maintenance was conducted.

Voice
Carte Blanche has been approached by several insiders, all former CemAir employees, who say that maintenance problems are too common for comfort at the airline. This man, who we’ll call “Joseph”, says maintenance staff are pressured into quick turn around times.

Sound Up “Joseph”
Devi: When you heard that the CAA was grounding CemAir’s planes as a result of safety clearance issues, were you surprised?

Joseph: No I wasn’t surprised to hear that. Their maintenance staff are put under extreme pressure by management to get those aeroplanes up and running. If an aeroplane is down, it costs the company money.

Voice
Joseph alleges CemAir often skimp on safety precautions.

Sound UP Joseph
They are an airline that has a lot going, but to me, it’s all at the expense of safety.

Voice
van der Molen denies that CemAir do not take safety issues such as maintenance seriously, and says the current circumstances the company finds itself in is as a result of a malicious smear campaign.

Sound Up Miles
We certainly have been targeted, we are working our way into a very difficult industry, and we are watched very closely.

Voice
But Joseph says he has seen aircraft maintenance being rushed.

Sound Up Joseph
Often, the crews, when they have a massive inspection, will be pressed to do a three day maintenance inspection in 24 hours you know, or in a far lesser period there.

Link Devi
In aviation safety is paramount. Aircraft are engineered to have multiple failsafes, but if operators break the rules, passenger’s lives are at stake.

Voice Over
Joseph says the overloading of aircraft is another dangerous practice that happens both locally and in Cemair’s African operations.

Sound Up Joseph
And overloading is a common practice, especially in Sudan. The crews actually plan to land overweight.

Voice
Carte Blanche has seen multiple emails, internal CemAir reports and documents where overweight aircraft locally and abroad are discussed and reported to CemAir executives. Another insider, who we’ll call Brandon, says although the concerns are reported to management they are sooner forgotten then dealt with.

Sound Up Brandon
It’s been reported by several people, and then basically was just swept under the rug and when it came back to the crew who had reported it they were told well this is the way it’s done here, if you don’t like it, leave.

Voice
van der Molen denies that CemAir overload their planes.

Sound Up Miles
Devi: Has any CemAir aircraft ever taken off overloaded?

Miles: It’s a very categorical question, our policies are very clear. And the captain is responsible for the loading of the aircraft. But something could of happened beyond my knowledge, I can’t speak for what I haven’t seen.

Voice
So we read him an example of a document from his own internal safety reporting system that he would have knowledge of. In it a pilot, who is not one of our insiders, complains that last year a CemAir plane taking off from OR Tambo International was overloaded. He also raises concerns about the fuelling. The captain responsible for checking the loading of the craft? Miles van der Molen.

Sound Up Miles
Devi: So he says here that he expressed his concerns to capt van der Molen that fuel was going to be an issue without stopping in Bloem to refuel. Shortly after arriving at the aircraft I was called aside by the captain and asked why I was being difficult and if I doubted his workings. I was told that if I was not happy I could go home, to which I replied I would do so as I disagreed with the way he had worked out the baggage load for pax. As I started to walk away I was then threatened that if I was proved wrong captain would be after me and my job. Result is we took off overweight by 464 pounds, excluding the weight of 7 dogs and their associated carrier weights. I find it totally unacceptable that crew get bullied and threatened with their jobs for wanting to stick to the laws and operate safely. Is he lying?

Miles: He boarded that flight and flew as a passenger at the back.

Devi: Is he lying?

Miles: Yes. If it was unsafe, why did he board the flight as a passenger. My words to him were, if you think we are overweight you can be the first 200 pounds that we save.

Miles: Yes. If it was unsafe, why did he board the flight as a passenger. My words to him were, if you think we are overweight you can be the first 200 pounds that we save.

Voice
Van der Molen says the pilot’s weight calculations were wrong, and that van der Molen’s were correct.

Link Devi
Insiders claim the company culture at CemAir is one of fear and intimidation. According to them, speaking out has resulted in people losing their jobs.

Sound Up “Joseph”
Devi: People are talking about this company culture that’s based on fear and people being pressurised into doing things that are illegal. Is that a fair comment?

Joseph: It is a very fair comment. The fear based culture in that company is very, very strong.

Sound Up Miles
Miles: The company culture is one of discipline and structure. People that don’t want to follow the structure, don’t do well in this environment.

Voice
Van der Molen says he encourages reporting from his crew, and that the documents we’ve seen prove that.But Brandon says it’s no use to report safety concerns if they are only going to be used as ammunition against you.

Sound Up “Brandon”
You know these guys are under a massive amount of pressure from Miles to comply. If you stand up to them either you get fired, or you get a written warning or you know the company’s got a political hierarchy, so you’ll end up being made a first officer again, or there will be some form of punitive situation.

Voice
Our insiders say the concerns they’ve raised about CemAir can lead to lethal consequences, and that van der Molen should be the first to realise that. In 1999, van der Molen and his then company Flightline Charter Services owned and operated a Piper Chieftain which crashed shortly after take-off from Rand Airport in Johannesburg. All ten people on board were killed.

Sound Up Miles
Devi: So a magistrate found negligence.

Miles: During an inquest. Negligence was cited, yes.

Devi: Negligence on whose part?

Miles: Several people’s part and I was on the list.

Devi: But you’re not responsible? You were found negligent, together with other people, but you were not responsible?

Miles: I was responsible for the aircraft. We were the operator. So responsible for the aircraft and responsible for the accident are slightly different things.

Voice
Part of a CAA report on the tragedy reads: The precipitative cause of this accident was the failure of the exhaust pipe segment, which caused the right hand engine to lose power/fail. The aircraft was also overloaded and consequently was unable to maintain altitude. Van der Molen says our insiders are simply disgruntled employees who could not make it in the CemAir corporate culture.

Sound Up Miles
Devi: Why do you think then that people are so unhappy with you?

Miles: Well there are a lot of people that we pushed out because they were the wrong material for us. We have an airline environment, we are looking to move to a more structured, more disciplined way, and we had some crew that that way didn’t suit them.

Devi: Sour grapes?

Miles: Ja.

Sound Up Brandon
Devi: Why did you leave?

Brandon: Because of the overloading of the aircraft, and the lack of anything being done about it.

Voice
The CAA have said they will not allow CemAir to get airborne until they have resolved their current investigation. Meanwhile they would not confirm the nature of any other investigations into Cemair, but they did verify that there are ongoing enquiries into the airline related to anonymous tip-offs they received last year.
